description: I am a software engineer from Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan, building Orbisol, a decision-support tool for the Field Shift challenge. It helps farmers make informed crop-rotation decisions as temperatures, rainfall and water availability change, using NASA Earth observation data. I work with React, TypeScript and Python, and my aim is to support climate-resilient agriculture in Sindh.
summary: Every April, thousands of fields around Hyderabad, Sindh lie bare in the hottest weeks of the year: wheat is cut, cotton is not yet sown, and sun and wind take the topsoil. NASA's MODIS satellite sees it happen. Orbisol turns that view into a decision. A farmer pins a field and says how they farm now: rotation, canal-water turn, soil and priorities. Orbisol uses six NASA datasets to show how this season compares with 30 years of normal, when the field is bare and crops are vulnerable, and how heat may change by 2050. It then compares the current rotation with two alternatives, for example sorghum fodder then berseem, which needs about 12% less water (about 1 in 8 canal turns), and states the trade-offs honestly. Every number shows its source and date, a 60-second guided tour explains the app, and it works offline on a low-end phone. Orbisol supports, not replaces, the farmer's judgment.
details:
Why I built this: I grew up in Sindh, where most families live from canal-irrigated farming. Farmers here decide rotations from habit and word of mouth, while NASA watches every field from space. I wanted to put that data in a farmer's hand, in plain words, on a cheap phone.

What it does: A farmer pins a field (GPS, map, village search or demo) and tells Orbisol the current rotation, canal turn (warabandi), soil type (incl. salty) and up to three priorities (water use, forage, nitrogen-fixing, erosion, organic matter, market). Orbisol then shows: (1) Overview - the key findings in plain words; (2) Rotations - the existing rotation plus two alternatives ranked by the farmer's priorities, with water use relative to the current rotation, bare days, legume days, Water Fit against the canal turn, salt tolerance, cited notes on pest cycles, infiltration and fodder income, and why / evidence / benefits / gaps / risks; (3) Calendar - a crop-year timeline with bare-field gaps, the hottest months and the MODIS greenness curve; (4) Season - this season vs the 1991-2020 normal (hot days, rain, extreme rain, frost, soil wetness, evaporation demand, water balance), satellite rain, Season Twins (most similar past years), a Confidence Meter, a Track Record backtest against a naive guess, observed trends and a 2050 heat outlook.

How it works: live NASA POWER daily data (1990-now) for any pin on Earth; FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration and crop coefficients for crop water need; WMO-style median normals and terciles; ETCCDI-style indicators; analog years with z-scores; leave-one-out backtesting. Heavy satellite products are precomputed by a Python pipeline into small JSON for the Hyderabad case study. Every number shows its source, kind (satellite / model / reference / farmer input) and date.

Global reach: works for any field on Earth today using live NASA POWER data; tested live for Hyderabad (Sindh) and Faisalabad (Punjab). A 60-second guided tour and a 12-month NASA MODIS time-lapse help first-time users.

Benefits and impact: farmers see risks such as bare soil in the hottest weeks and canal turns that are too long for the crop, and explore rotations that save water or add fodder and legumes, while the app marks where local expertise must decide. Works on low-end phones and offline after first use.

Creativity: Season Twins, an honest Track Record against a naive baseline, Water Fit against the real canal-turn system, and NASA's MODIS satellite confirming the bare-soil gap that the crop calendar predicts.

Tools: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, PWA (Workbox), MapLibre GL, React Router, TanStack Query, Zustand, Zod, Dexie (IndexedDB), i18next, Phosphor icons, Vitest (74 tests); Python (requests, pandas, xarray); hosted on Vercel.
